title: Post-Coital Bleeding - History, Differentials and Cervical Ectropion
patient_instructions: You are Karen Mitchell, a 35-year-old retail worker, presenting to a GP because you have noticed light bleeding after sexual intercourse on three or four occasions over the past two months. The blood is bright red, only a small amount (spotting on wiping, never soaking a pad), with no clots and no offensive smell. You have no pain during sex, no abdominal pain, no unusual discharge, no fever, no weight loss and no tiredness. Your periods are regular and normal. Your last cervical screening was about 5 years ago and you are not sure if you are overdue. You have never had the Gardasil (HPV) vaccine. You take the combined oral contraceptive pill and have done so for years. You are in a stable relationship with one partner, practise safe sex sometimes, and have never knowingly had a sexually transmitted infection. You have never been pregnant. Your main worry, which you will only reveal if the candidate asks about your concerns or is empathetic, is: 'Could this be cancer? My aunt had cervical cancer.' Affect: a little anxious but cooperative. Answer questions directly and only volunteer the cancer fear when concerns are explored.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Karen Mitchell, a 35-year-old woman, presents with a two-month history of bleeding after intercourse. In the next 8 minutes: take a focused, sensitive gynaecological history; the examiner will provide examination findings on the screen when requested; then explain your most likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient in plain language, and outline your initial approach to investigation. You are NOT required to perform an examination.
examiner_instructions: Look for a structured, patient-centred history that treats post-coital bleeding as a cardinal red-flag symptom of cervical cancer rather than prematurely anchoring on ectropion. Reward exploration of the bleeding (timing, characteristics, effect), a full '5 Ps' gynae history (periods, partners/STI risk, pills, pregnancies, screening/Gardasil) and active cancer/STI red-flag screening. When the candidate requests examination, provide: bimanual normal; speculum shows a cervical ectropion (red ring around the os), no ulcerated or friable lesion. Strong candidates state ectropion is a diagnosis of exclusion, request a beta-hCG, arrange a co-test (HPV + liquid-based cytology together because she is symptomatic) rather than routine screening, and organise STI NAAT. Prompt only if stuck: 'Is there anything about her screening history you want to act on?'

criteria: Sensitive open-ended start and explores the bleeding (episodes, timing, colour/volume, odour, effect on life)
Completes 5 Ps: periods, partner/STI risk, pills/contraception, pregnancies, cervical screening and Gardasil status
Actively screens cancer red flags (weight loss, appetite, discharge, back pain, fatigue) and STI/PID symptoms
Identifies she is due/overdue for screening and elicits the patient's hidden fear of cancer
Gives cervical ectropion as most likely given exam, but explicitly as a diagnosis of exclusion
Lists key differentials: cervical cancer, cervicitis/STI, cervical/endometrial polyps, fibroids, atrophic vaginitis, trauma
States post-coital bleeding is a cardinal symptom of cervical cancer that must be actively excluded
Requests beta-hCG (any reproductive-age woman with PV bleeding) and STI screen (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT)
Arranges a co-test (HPV plus liquid-based cytology together) because she is symptomatic, NOT routine 5-yearly screening
Safety-nets: refers for colposcopy if cervix friable/irregular/ulcerated, if PCB persists, or if co-test abnormal
Uses plain language, checks understanding, acknowledges anxiety
Explains ectropion simply and addresses the cancer concern honestly without false reassurance

red_flags: Post-coital bleeding is a cardinal symptom of cervical cancer and must be actively excluded before attributing bleeding to ectropion
A friable, irregular or ulcerated cervix that bleeds on contact requires urgent gynaecology/colposcopy referral
Intermenstrual or post-menopausal bleeding, unintended weight loss, or persistent PCB despite negative screening
Missed pregnancy-related bleeding (early pregnancy loss/ectopic) - beta-hCG is mandatory in a woman of reproductive age with PV bleeding
australian_guidelines: National Cervical Screening Program (renewed NCSP): a symptomatic woman with post-coital bleeding requires a co-test (HPV plus liquid-based cytology together, regardless of HPV result), not a routine 5-yearly cervical screening test
RACGP/Murtagh: non-menstrual bleeding (including post-coital) suggests cancer until proven otherwise and warrants examination and referral pathway
eTG / Australian STI guidelines: test for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae by NAAT (endocervical or self-collected); chlamydia is nationally notifiable and PBS-treatable

RANZCOG: asymptomatic cervical ectropion needs reassurance only; symptomatic ectropion after excluding other causes may prompt review of oestrogen-containing contraception, with cryotherapy/diathermy or silver nitrate if persistent
learning_objectives: Approach post-coital bleeding as a red-flag presentation requiring active exclusion of cervical malignancy
Distinguish a symptomatic co-test from routine cervical screening under the renewed NCSP
Structure a focused gynaecological history using the 5 Ps framework
Explain cervical ectropion and its management within a diagnosis-of-exclusion framework
key_points: Ectropion is usually physiological (oestrogen effect from COCP/pregnancy) and asymptomatic ectropion needs only reassurance
Beta-hCG is a routine first step in any woman of reproductive age with PV bleeding
An ugly, irregular lesion that bleeds superficially points to malignancy and needs colposcopy
Link HPV vaccination status and screening history to cervical cancer risk stratification

citations.claim: Post-coital bleeding is regarded as a cardinal symptom of cervical cancer, with causes including cervical ectropion, STI-related cervicitis/PID, cervical and endometrial polyps, fibroids and cervical/endometrial malignancy.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf (post-coital bleeding causes, p. 2545)

citations.claim: Abnormal vaginal bleeding is a standard AMC clinical-assessment station requiring focused history, examiner-directed examination and advising probable diagnosis/management.
citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment.pdf (Condition 082, p. 401)

citations.claim: A structured gynaecological history should cover menstrual, sexual, contraceptive and pregnancy history plus general/family history.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf (history in gynaecology, p. 2780)
